title: Repentance, Faith and Conversion
summary: What it means to turn from sin and trust Christ: the human response to the gospel and the new birth that lies behind it.
description: How does a person become a Christian? This course explains conversion as turning from sin (repentance) to Christ (faith), shows how both are gifts of grace and duties of every hearer, describes the new birth that makes conversion possible, and helps learners recognise true and false conversion and lead others to Christ.
objectives: Define conversion, repentance and saving faith
Explain the relationship between regeneration and conversion
Distinguish true repentance from mere regret
Equip learners to lead others to repentance and faith
outcomes: Explain the three elements of saving faith
Describe the fruits of true repentance
Show how new birth and conversion relate
Present the gospel call to repent and believe

modules.title: Turning Around
modules.intro: Conversion means turning. This week we see what conversion is and why every person needs it.

lessons.title: What is conversion?
lessons.body:
To convert means to turn. The Thessalonians "turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God" (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Conversion has two sides: turning **from** sin (repentance) and turning **to** Christ (faith).

Peter preached, "Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out" (Acts 3:19). Paul testified "repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ" (Acts 20:21).

Jesus said, "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 18:3). Conversion is not optional.

lessons.title: Why conversion is needed
lessons.body:
Everyone needs to turn because "all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Religious upbringing, church membership or good deeds cannot replace it.

Nicodemus was a respected religious teacher, yet Jesus told him, "Ye must be born again" (John 3:7). Paul was zealous and blameless in outward law-keeping, yet counted it all loss to gain Christ (Philippians 3:4-9).

Children of believers are blessed to hear the gospel early, but each person must personally repent and believe (John 1:12-13).

lessons.title: Conversion stories
lessons.body:
Conversions in Scripture differ in their circumstances but share the same heart.

- **Zacchaeus** received Jesus joyfully and repaid those he had cheated (Luke 19:1-10).
- **The Philippian jailer** asked, "what must I do to be saved?" and was told, "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Acts 16:30-31).
- **Saul** met the risen Christ dramatically on the Damascus road (Acts 9:1-19).
- **Timothy** knew the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15).

Some conversions are sudden, others gradual. What matters is not the drama but real repentance and faith.

modules.title: True Repentance
modules.intro: Repentance is more than feeling sorry. This week we study what it involves and how it shows.

lessons.title: A change of mind, heart and life
lessons.body:
The Greek word for repentance, *metanoia*, means a change of mind. But biblical repentance involves the whole person:

- **Mind**: seeing sin as God sees it (Psalm 51:3-4).
- **Heart**: grieving over sin as an offence against God (2 Corinthians 7:10).
- **Will**: forsaking sin and turning to God (Isaiah 55:7).

"He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Proverbs 28:13). Repentance confesses and forsakes.

lessons.title: Godly sorrow and worldly sorrow
lessons.body:
"For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death" (2 Corinthians 7:10).

**Worldly sorrow** regrets the consequences of sin: being caught, shame, loss. Judas felt remorse and returned the money, but he did not turn to God (Matthew 27:3-5). Esau wept for the lost blessing, not for his sin (Hebrews 12:17).

**Godly sorrow** grieves that we have sinned against God. Peter wept bitterly after denying Jesus and was restored (Luke 22:62; John 21:15-17). David cried, "Against thee, thee only, have I sinned" (Psalm 51:4).

lessons.title: Fruits meet for repentance
lessons.body:
John the Baptist demanded, "Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance" (Matthew 3:8). Real repentance shows in changed behaviour.

When the crowds asked what to do, John told them to share with the needy, stop extortion and be content with wages (Luke 3:10-14). Zacchaeus restored fourfold what he had taken (Luke 19:8). The Ephesian believers burned their magic books (Acts 19:18-19).

Restitution, where possible, is a mark of sincere repentance. Repentance is also ongoing: believers keep confessing sin and receiving cleansing (1 John 1:9).

terms.def: A change of mind, heart and life: turning from sin to God.
The Greek word for repentance, meaning a change of mind.

summary: Repentance involves mind, heart and will.
Godly sorrow grieves sin against God; worldly sorrow only regrets consequences.

modules.title: Saving Faith
modules.intro: Faith is the hand that receives Christ. This week we study what saving faith is and what it is not.

lessons.title: Knowledge, agreement and trust
lessons.body:
Saving faith has three parts:

1. **Knowledge**: knowing the facts of the gospel. "How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard?" (Romans 10:14).
2. **Assent**: agreeing that they are true.
3. **Trust**: personally relying on Christ. Paul said, "I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him" (2 Timothy 1:12).

Knowledge and agreement alone are not enough: "the devils also believe, and tremble" (James 2:19). Saving faith is resting the whole weight of our soul on Christ.

lessons.title: Faith in Christ alone
lessons.body:
Faith saves not because of its strength but because of its object. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves; strong faith in a false saviour cannot.

"Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). We trust Christ alone, not Christ plus our works, rituals, charms or ancestors.

Faith receives a gift: "as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name" (John 1:12). It is the empty hand that takes what God offers.

lessons.title: Faith that works
lessons.body:
Saving faith is never alone; it produces obedience and love. James says, "faith, if it hath not works, is dead" (James 2:17). Paul speaks of "faith which worketh by love" (Galatians 5:6).

Paul and James do not contradict each other. Paul teaches that we are saved by faith apart from works (Romans 3:28). James teaches that real faith shows itself in works (James 2:18). Works are the fruit, not the root, of salvation.

Faith also grows: "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God" (Romans 10:17). The disciples prayed, "Lord, increase our faith" (Luke 17:5).

The part of faith that knows the facts of the gospel.
The part of faith that agrees the gospel is true.
The part of faith that personally relies on Christ.
The one in whom faith rests; for saving faith, Christ alone.
Mere profession without the fruit of good works (James 2:17).

Faith without works is dead.

summary: Saving faith includes knowledge, assent and personal trust.
Faith saves because of its object: Christ alone.
True faith works by love; works are fruit, not root.

modules.title: New Birth and True Conversion
modules.intro: Behind conversion is God's work of new birth. This week we see how they relate, how to recognise genuine conversion, and how to lead others to Christ.

lessons.title: Regeneration and conversion
lessons.body:
**Regeneration** is God's work: the Spirit giving new life (John 3:5-8). **Conversion** is our response: repenting and believing. They happen together in experience.

Which comes first in logical order? Calvinists say regeneration comes first, so that a dead sinner can believe (Ephesians 2:5). Arminians say prevenient grace enables faith, and regeneration follows faith (John 1:12-13). Both agree that God takes the initiative and that the result is a new creature: "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature" (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Both repentance and faith are gifts (Acts 11:18; Ephesians 2:8) and commands (Acts 17:30).

lessons.title: Marks of true conversion
lessons.body:
Not everyone who says "Lord, Lord" truly knows Christ (Matthew 7:21-23). In the parable of the sower, some receive the word with joy but fall away (Matthew 13:20-22).

First John gives tests of genuine new birth:

- Believing that Jesus is the Christ (1 John 5:1).
- Keeping His commandments (2:3-4).
- Not continuing in a lifestyle of sin (3:9).
- Loving fellow believers (3:14).

These marks are not perfection but direction. The aim is not to make believers doubt, but to help them "know that ye have eternal life" (5:13).

lessons.title: Calling others to repent and believe
lessons.body:
Jesus' first message was "Repent ye, and believe the gospel" (Mark 1:15). We should call people to both.

A simple way to lead someone to Christ:

1. Explain God's holiness and our sin (Romans 3:23).
2. Explain Christ's death and resurrection for sinners (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).
3. Call them to turn from sin and trust Christ (Acts 3:19).
4. Encourage them to confess Christ (Romans 10:9-10), be baptized and join a church.

Avoid pressure or easy formulas. Pray, explain clearly, and trust the Spirit to convict and give new life.

terms.def: God's work of giving new spiritual life by the Holy Spirit.

summary: Regeneration is God's work; conversion is our response; they occur together.
Repentance and faith are both gifts and commands.
First John gives marks of genuine new birth.

short.q: Define conversion and name its two sides.
short.model: Conversion is turning from sin to God; its two sides are repentance and faith.

short.q: Distinguish godly sorrow from worldly sorrow, with an example of each.
short.model: Godly sorrow grieves sin as against God and leads to repentance, as with Peter or David; worldly sorrow only regrets consequences, as with Judas or Esau.

short.q: What are fruits meet for repentance? Give an example.
short.model: Changed behaviour that shows repentance is real, such as Zacchaeus' restitution.

short.q: Explain the three parts of saving faith.
short.model: Knowledge of the gospel, assent that it is true, and personal trust in Christ.

short.q: How do Paul and James agree on faith and works?
short.model: Paul teaches we are saved by faith apart from works; James teaches that true faith shows itself in works. Works are fruit, not root.

short.q: How are regeneration and conversion related?
short.model: Regeneration is God giving new life; conversion is our response of repentance and faith; they happen together.

assignments.title: My conversion
assignments.prompt: Write your own testimony of coming to Christ. Then examine it in the light of this course: where do you see repentance, faith and new birth? Use at least four passages from the course.

assignments.title: Leading a friend to Christ
assignments.prompt: Write the conversation you would have with a friend who says, "I have been in church all my life; surely I am a Christian." Explain conversion, repentance and saving faith clearly, using at least five Bible passages.
